2a.html:
Import substitution industrialisation (ISI) is an inward-looking policy: the country replaces imported manufactures with domestic production for the home market, behind protection.

  • Stages: first simple consumer goods (textiles, soap, bicycles), then intermediate and capital goods (steel, chemicals, machinery).
  • Instruments: tariffs, quotas, import licensing and an overvalued exchange rate that cheapens imported machinery.
  • Rationale: infant-industry protection until scale economies and learning by doing lower costs; saving foreign exchange.
  • Examples: India, Pakistan and Latin America in the 1950s and 1960s.

Export promotion (EP) is an outward-looking policy: government raises export incentives and removes disincentives, to expand exports and earn foreign exchange.

  • Instruments: export subsidies, duty drawback, bonded warehouses, export processing zones and a competitive exchange rate.
  • Scope: primary or manufactured exports.
  • Examples: South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore; Bangladesh's ready-made garments.

The two are not exclusive: East Asian exporters protected some industries first, then pushed them into world markets.
pts: Defines ISI: replacing imported manufactures by domestic production for the home market, behind protection (inward-looking)
ISI stages (consumer goods, then intermediate and capital goods) and instruments (tariffs, quotas, licensing, overvalued exchange rate), with the infant-industry rationale
Defines EP: outward-looking policy of raising export incentives and removing disincentives to expand exports and earn foreign exchange
EP instruments, for example export subsidies, duty drawback, bonded warehouses, EPZs or a competitive exchange rate; primary or manufactured exports
Examples: ISI in Latin America or South Asia; EP in the East Asian economies or Bangladesh's RMG
Notes that the two are often combined or sequenced (ISI first, then EP)
2a.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 686-688, 692-694, 704-707
2a.watch:
• "What do you understand by" asks for meaning, not an evaluation: keep the arguments for each policy for part (b).
  • Do not confuse EP with free trade: the successful exporters used active, targeted government support.

2b.html:
The debate is between the trade optimists, who favour outward-looking export promotion (EP), and the trade pessimists, who favour inward-looking import substitution (ISI).

Arguments for export promotion

  1. Efficiency and comparative advantage. Competition in world markets forces firms to cut costs and allocates resources to goods the country makes cheaply, such as labour-intensive manufactures.
  2. Scale and technology. The world market is far larger than the home market, so firms reach economies of scale; foreign buyers pass on designs, quality standards and know-how, which raises productivity.
  3. Foreign exchange. Export earnings ease the balance of payments and pay for imported machinery, fuel and food.
  4. Foreign capital and fewer distortions. An open economy attracts FDI and expertise, and avoids the rent-seeking and corruption of import licences and controls.
  5. Jobs and evidence. Labour-intensive exports create many jobs: Taiwan's exports grew over 20% a year for decades (South Korea's faster), and Bangladesh's garment industry employs about 4 million workers, mostly women.

Arguments for import substitution

  1. Infant industry. A new industry has high costs at first; a temporary tariff lets it reach scale economies and learning by doing until it can compete, preparing later exports.
  2. Export pessimism. Primary exports have low income and price elasticities of demand (0.3 to 0.6 for tea, coffee and sugar), face synthetic substitutes, and suffer falling terms of trade (the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis).
  3. New protectionism. Rich countries put tariffs, quotas and non-tariff barriers on developing countries' manufactures (for example the Multifibre Arrangement), so export markets are uncertain.
  4. Balance of payments. Producing at home what was imported saves scarce foreign exchange.
  5. Diversification and self-reliance. ISI builds an industrial base with linkages and skills, cuts dependence on a few primary exports, and raises easy tariff revenue.

Conclusion: the East Asian record favours EP, but those countries also protected selected industries first; the arguments point to a sequenced, export-oriented strategy with selective, time-limited protection.
pts: EP: competition and specialisation by comparative advantage raise efficiency and cut costs
EP: large world market gives economies of scale and learning from foreign buyers (technology, quality)
EP: earns foreign exchange for imports of capital goods and food, easing the balance of payments
EP: attracts foreign capital and expertise, or removes distortions and rent-seeking of controls
EP: labour-intensive employment, with East Asian or Bangladesh RMG evidence
ISI: infant-industry argument (temporary protection until scale economies and learning by doing lower costs)
ISI: export pessimism: low elasticities of demand for primary goods, synthetics, Prebisch-Singer terms-of-trade decline
ISI: new protectionism in developed countries against manufactured exports
ISI: saves foreign exchange and improves the balance of payments
ISI: diversification, industrial base and linkages, self-reliance or tariff revenue
2b.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 688-694, 704-707
2b.watch:
• The question asks for the arguments for each policy; the failures of ISI in practice (inefficient protected firms, worse balance of payments, overvalued currency hurting farmers) belong only in a one-line conclusion.
  • The 4 million RMG workers figure is a slide figure from the population deck (hum-ch6 slide 46); other sources give 3.5 to 4.5 million.
  • Trade pessimists and optimists are Todaro's labels; the examiner may also accept "inward-looking" and "outward-looking".

3a.html:
Private foreign investment (PFI) is profit-seeking investment in a country by foreign private firms or individuals, as distinct from official aid or loans. It takes two forms:

  1. Foreign direct investment (FDI): equity investment, usually by a multinational corporation, giving lasting management control (by convention 10% or more of voting shares): a new plant, a takeover or a joint venture.
  2. Portfolio investment: purchases of shares and bonds without control; liquid, so it can leave quickly ("hot money").

FDI brings a package of capital, technology and management, and part of its profit is repatriated; examples are Grameenphone (Telenor) and Chevron in Bangladesh.
pts: Defines PFI: profit-seeking investment by foreign private firms or individuals, as distinct from official aid or loans
FDI: equity with management control (about 10% or more of voting shares), usually by MNCs; greenfield, takeover or joint venture
Portfolio investment: shares and bonds without control, liquid and volatile
Notes the FDI package (capital, technology, management) or profit repatriation
3a.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 791-795, 802-803
3a.watch:
• Foreign aid is official (public) finance; do not mix it into PFI.
  • Remittances are private inflows but not investment.

3b.html:
The traditional case for private foreign investment (PFI) is that it fills four gaps between the resources a developing country has and those it needs for its growth targets.

  1. Savings-investment gap. In the Harrod-Domar model g = s/k, so the saving rate needed is s = g\,k: for a 7% target and k = 3, s = 21\% of GDP; with 16% domestic saving, foreign capital fills the 5% gap.
  2. Foreign-exchange gap. FDI brings in foreign currency and, if the firm exports, earns more over time, easing the current-account deficit.
  3. Government revenue gap. Taxes on the profits of foreign firms and the incomes they create raise public revenue for development spending.
  4. Management, technology and skills gap. A multinational brings a package: modern machinery, production know-how, managerial and marketing skills and overseas contacts. Local staff learn by doing, and the knowledge spreads when trained workers start their own firms or when the firm trains local suppliers (vertical spillovers).

Other roles: modern-sector jobs, access to global value chains and export markets, and more competition for local firms, as in Bangladesh's export processing zones.

Conclusion: PFI helps development when the foreign firm's interests coincide with national priorities; host-country policy (performance requirements, linkage and training programmes) decides how much of the benefit stays.
pts: Frames the role as filling resource gaps (savings, foreign exchange, revenue, skills)
Savings gap via Harrod-Domar, s = g k: required saving exceeds domestic saving and PFI fills the difference (a numerical example is optional)
Foreign-exchange gap: inflows and export earnings ease the balance of payments
Government revenue gap: taxes on profits and incomes
Technology, management and skills package, with learning by doing or spillovers to local firms
Jobs, access to export markets or global value chains, or competition
Concludes that the benefit depends on host policy and coinciding interests
3b.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 793-797, 801-802
3b.watch:
• Todaro's own numbers are the 7% target, k = 3 and 16% domestic saving; the example illustrates the gap but is not required.
  • Evidence on spillovers is mixed: little horizontal spillover to local competitors, but some vertical spillover to local suppliers.
  • "Role" is the positive case; the demerits are part (c).

3c.html:
Critics argue that private foreign investment can widen the very gaps it is meant to fill.

  1. Savings. It may replace local saving, borrow locally (crowding out local firms) and reinvest little profit.
  2. Foreign-exchange drain. Imported inputs (often from affiliates at inflated prices) and repatriated profits, royalties and fees can make the long-run balance negative.
  3. Less tax. Tax holidays won in a "race to the bottom" and transfer pricing (pricing trade between affiliates so profit appears in low-tax countries) cut revenue.
  4. Weak skill transfer. Research stays at home and dominant foreign firms stifle local entrepreneurs.
  5. Inappropriate technology. Capital-intensive methods create few jobs; products and advertising serve elites.
  6. Dualism. Investment clusters in urban enclaves, widening inequality and the urban-rural gap.
  7. Political power and volatility. Large firms can sway policy (ITT in Chile), and portfolio "hot money" can flee, as in the 1997 Asian crisis.
pts: May lower domestic saving and investment, crowd out local firms or reinvest little
Long-run foreign-exchange drain: imported inputs and repatriated profits, royalties and fees
Smaller tax contribution: concessions, race to the bottom or transfer pricing (defined)
Stifles local entrepreneurship; limited real transfer of technology and skills
Inappropriate capital-intensive technology with few jobs, or elite products and consumption patterns
Reinforces dualism, inequality and urban bias
Political influence over host governments, or volatility of portfolio flows
3c.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 793-799, 802-803
3c.watch:
• Each demerit is the mirror of a claimed benefit (savings, foreign exchange, revenue, skills); presenting them that way shows understanding.
  • These are possibilities, not certainties: Todaro concludes that the outcome depends on the bargaining power and policies of the host country.

4a.html:
A multinational corporation (MNC) is a corporation that conducts and controls productive activities in more than one country. MNCs are very large (the 100 biggest sold over USD 9 trillion in 2018), centrally controlled by a parent company, and usually oligopolists, which gives them strong bargaining power over small host countries. Examples in Bangladesh: Unilever, Grameenphone (Telenor), Chevron.

Merits

  1. Capital. MNC investment fills the savings-investment gap between the investment needed for a growth target and domestic saving.
  2. Foreign exchange and markets. Capital inflows and exports ease the balance of payments; MNCs open global markets and value chains to local producers.
  3. Tax revenue from their profits and the incomes they generate.
  4. Technology, management and skills. They bring modern machinery, production know-how and managerial and marketing skills; local workers learn by doing and suppliers are trained to meet standards.
  5. Jobs, linkages and competition. Modern-sector jobs, demand for local inputs, pressure on local firms to raise quality.

Demerits

  1. Foreign-exchange drain. Imported inputs (often from affiliates) and repatriated profits, royalties and fees can exceed the inflow over time.
  2. Lost revenue. Tax holidays won in a "race to the bottom" and transfer pricing (setting prices between affiliates so profits appear in tax havens) shrink the tax base.
  3. Inappropriate technology and products. Capital-intensive methods create few jobs; products and advertising serve elites; enclaves deepen dualism, inequality and urban bias.
  4. Crowding out. Superior finance and brands drive out local firms and stifle local entrepreneurship; R&D stays in the home country.
  5. Power and standards. MNCs can influence politics (ITT in Chile) and may tolerate poor labour or environmental conditions; the 2013 Rana Plaza collapse in Bangladesh led buyers to set up safety monitoring under pressure.

Conclusion: MNCs are neither saviours nor villains; they benefit the host country when its bargaining power and regulation (performance and local-content requirements, tax enforcement, labour standards) align their profit motive with development.
pts: Defines an MNC (production controlled in more than one country) with its features: size, central control, oligopoly power
Merit: fills the savings-investment gap
Merit: foreign exchange, exports and access to global markets
Merit: tax revenue
Merit: transfer of technology, management and skills (learning by doing, supplier training)
Merit: jobs, linkages to local suppliers or competition
Demerit: foreign-exchange drain through imported inputs and repatriated profits, royalties and fees
Demerit: lost revenue through tax concessions (race to the bottom) or transfer pricing
Demerit: inappropriate capital-intensive technology and products, dualism and inequality
Demerit: crowding out of local firms and entrepreneurship
Demerit: political influence, or weak labour and environmental standards
Concludes that the net effect depends on host-country bargaining and regulation
4a.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 791-802
4a.watch:
• Explain each merit and demerit with its reason; a bare list of words earns little.
  • Todaro's balanced conclusion: the debate rests on value judgements, and the gains are largest when host governments bargain jointly and set clear rules.
  • Grameenphone, Unilever and others are illustrations; any correctly described MNC example earns the credit.

5a.html:
The Lewis theory (W. Arthur Lewis, 1954; extended by Fei and Ranis) is a two-sector model in which surplus labour from traditional agriculture is transferred to a modern industrial sector, whose growth absorbs it, industrialises the economy and sustains development.

The two sectors

  • Traditional sector: overpopulated rural subsistence farming with fixed land and technology. There is surplus labour: the marginal product of labour, MP_{LA}, is zero, so workers can leave without loss of output. Output is shared equally, so rural income W_A equals the average product.
  • Modern sector: urban industry, where employers hire until the marginal product of labour equals the wage; the MP_{LM} curve is the labour demand curve.

The process

  1. The urban wage W_M is fixed at a premium over W_A; at that wage industry can hire unlimited rural labour, so the supply curve is horizontal.
  2. With capital K_{M1}, demand D_1 meets supply at F: employment L_1, wages 0W_MFL_1, profits W_MD_1F.
  3. Capitalists reinvest all profits: capital rises to K_{M2}, demand shifts to D_2 and employment grows to L_2 at the same wage; larger profits are reinvested again (D_3, L_3).
  4. Growth continues until the surplus is absorbed; at the Lewis turning point the supply curve turns upward and wages rise.

Result: structural transformation from rural agriculture to urban industry, at a pace set by modern-sector capital accumulation, as in Western history and recent Chinese growth.
pts: Defines the theory: surplus labour transferred from traditional agriculture to a growing modern industrial sector
Surplus labour with MP_{LA} = 0, removable without loss of output
Rural income W_A equals the average product (equal sharing), not the marginal product
Fixed urban wage W_M above W_A with an unlimited (horizontal) labour supply
Employment where MP_{LM} = W_M (in words or on a diagram), output split into wages and profits
All profits reinvested: capital rises, demand shifts out, employment grows at a constant wage
Lewis turning point: the surplus is exhausted, supply slopes upward and wages rise
Outcome: structural transformation from agriculture to industry
5a.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 22-26; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 163-166
5a.watch:
• Part (b) asks for the criticisms, so keep them out of this part.
  • Marks: printed as 13 1/3; the points total 13.5.
  • The rural income is the average product; the surplus is defined by a zero marginal product.

5b.html:
The model fits Western history, but several assumptions do not fit most developing countries today.

  1. Employment need not grow with capital. The model assumes job creation is proportional to capital accumulation. If profits buy labour-saving machines, the new labour demand curve is steeper and crosses the old one at the wage: output and profits rise, but employment stays at L_1. Profits may also leave as capital flight.
  2. Surplus labour is rural, full employment urban? Research finds little rural surplus labour (except seasonally), while cities have large open unemployment.
  3. Urban wages are not constant. Unions, civil-service pay scales and multinationals pushed urban wages up despite unemployment; such institutional factors have little role in the model.
  4. Diminishing returns in industry are assumed, but some industries show increasing returns.
  5. Neglect of agriculture and human capital. Without rising farm productivity, food becomes dearer and squeezes industrial profits; education and health are left out.

Conclusion: a valuable early picture of structural change that fits China (turning point about 2010), but it needs major modification elsewhere.
pts: Labour-saving reinvestment: output and profits rise but employment does not (crossing demand curves, in words or on a diagram), or profits lost to capital flight
Little surplus labour in rural areas, while urban unemployment is widespread
Urban wages rise through institutional forces (unions, pay scales, multinationals); institutions ignored
Increasing rather than diminishing returns in at least some modern-sector industries
Neglect of agricultural productivity or human capital, or another sound criticism
Conclusion: useful (the West, China) but needs modification
5b.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 27-28; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 166-168
5b.watch:
• The slides list four criticisms; numbers 1 to 4 above match them. The fifth is Todaro's (human capital) and the Fei-Ranis extension (agriculture).
  • For criticism 1, say what happens to output, wages and jobs; "technology is labour-saving" alone is not enough.

6a.fix: • hum-ch2 slides 14 and 20 say the education index uses a geometric mean and the maxima are the observed maxima. That was the 2010 to 2013 method. Since the 2014 Report the goalposts are fixed (85 yr, 18 yr, 15 yr, USD 75,000) and the education index is the arithmetic mean of the two schooling indices (hum-hdr p 2).
6a.html:
The Human Development Index (HDI) is UNDP's composite index, from 0 to 1, of a country's average achievement in a long and healthy life, knowledge, and a decent standard of living.

Step 1: dimension indices. Each indicator is scaled between fixed goalposts:

I = \frac{\text{actual value} - \text{minimum}}{\text{maximum} - \text{minimum}}
  • Health: life expectancy at birth, goalposts 20 and 85 years.
  • Education: expected years of schooling (0 to 18) and mean years of schooling (0 to 15); the education index I_E is the arithmetic mean of the two.
  • Income: GNI per capita at 2011 purchasing power parity (PPP: rates that equalise the cost of a common basket), USD 100 to 75,000, in natural logs (diminishing marginal utility): I_I = (\ln \mathrm{GNI} - \ln 100)/(\ln 75000 - \ln 100).

Step 2: geometric mean of the three indices.

\mathrm{HDI} = \left(I_H \times I_E \times I_I\right)^{1/3}

The dimensions are imperfect substitutes, so poor performance in any one pulls the HDI down.

Example (Bangladesh, HDR 2019): I_H = (72.3-20)/65 = 0.805, I_E = (11.2/18 + 6.1/15)/2 = 0.514, I_I = \ln(4057/100)/\ln 750 = 0.559, so \mathrm{HDI} = (0.805 \times 0.514 \times 0.559)^{1/3} = 0.614.

Classes: very high 0.800 and above, high 0.700 to 0.799, medium 0.550 to 0.699, low below 0.550; Bangladesh is medium.
pts: Defines the HDI: a composite 0 to 1 index of health, knowledge and living standard
Names the four indicators: life expectancy at birth, expected and mean years of schooling, GNI per capita at PPP
Dimension index = (actual - minimum)/(maximum - minimum), with goalposts 20 to 85 yr, 0 to 18, 0 to 15 and USD 100 to 75,000 (the slides' observed maxima also accepted)
Education index as the mean of the two schooling indices (arithmetic, or the slides' geometric version)
Income index in natural logs because of diminishing marginal utility of income
\mathrm{HDI} = (I_H I_E I_I)^{1/3}, the geometric mean of the three indices
Geometric mean: imperfect substitutability, so a weak dimension pulls the HDI down
Works an example through to the HDI, for example Bangladesh 0.614 or the slides' Ghana 0.558
States the classes with cut-offs 0.800, 0.700 and 0.550
6a.src: Ch 2 Comparative development, slides 13-20; HDR 2019 technical notes, pp 2-3; Dimensions of economic development (v3), slides 15-19; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 89-90, 144
6a.watch:
• The Ghana example (hum-ch2 slide 19) uses the 2010 to 2013 version: observed maxima of 83.6 yr, 13.3 yr and USD 87,478, and a geometric-mean education index divided by 0.971 (HDI 0.558). Either version earns credit if the goalposts are stated; do not mix them.
  • Only income is logged. An index cannot exceed 1: income above USD 75,000 is capped.
  • 0.614 is the 2018 value. The latest value on hum-dim slide 20 is 0.670 (rank 129 of 193), still medium.
  • The traditional HDI (1990 to 2009) was the arithmetic mean of life expectancy (25 to 85 yr), education (2/3 adult literacy + 1/3 gross enrolment) and log GDP per capita (USD 100 to 40,000); Bangladesh 2007 gave 0.543 (hum-todaro p 144).

6b.html:
Inequality (relative)

  • Size distribution: rank people by income and give each quintile's share. In Table 5.1 the bottom 40% gets 14% and the top 20% gets 51%; the Kuznets ratio (top 20% over bottom 40%) is 3.64.
  • Lorenz curve: cumulative % of income against cumulative % of population; the more it bows below the diagonal, the more unequal.
  • Gini coefficient: G = A/(A+B), from 0 (equality) to 1; Table 5.1 gives 0.44.

Poverty (absolute), against a poverty line Y_p:

  • Headcount ratio H/N: the share of people below the line.
  • Total poverty gap \mathrm{TPG} = \sum_{i=1}^{H} (Y_p - Y_i): the income needed to lift every poor person to the line; per head \mathrm{APG} = \mathrm{TPG}/N.
  • FGT index P_\alpha = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{H}\left(\frac{Y_p - Y_i}{Y_p}\right)^{\alpha}: \alpha = 0 headcount, 1 poverty gap, 2 severity.
  • MPI = H \times A: headcount times average intensity of deprivation in health, education and living standard; Bangladesh 2014: 0.413 \times 0.474 = 0.196.
pts: Size distribution by quintile or decile shares, or the Kuznets ratio (for example 51/14 = 3.64)
Lorenz curve: cumulative income against cumulative population, bow below the diagonal shows inequality
Gini = A/(A+B), 0 to 1, with an example value
Headcount ratio H/N
Poverty gap (TPG, APG or NPG) measuring the depth of poverty
FGT P_\alpha with \alpha = 0, 1, 2 meanings, illustrated (for example P_0 = 0.5, P_1 = 0.15, P_2 = 0.05)
MPI = H \times A over health, education and living standard
6b.src: Ch 5 Poverty and inequality, slides 6-29, 48-53; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 263-273
6b.watch:
• "Illustrate" asks for examples or diagrams, not only names: one number or sketch per measure.
  • Inequality measures are relative; poverty measures need a poverty line and are absolute.
  • The headcount ratio ignores how far below the line the poor are; P_2 satisfies monotonicity and distributional sensitivity.

6c.html:
Kuznets' inverted-U hypothesis: as GNI per capita rises, inequality (for example the Gini) first rises in the early stages of growth and later falls, tracing an inverted U.

Why. Early growth is concentrated in a small high-wage modern sector (Lewis-type modern-sector enlargement); returns to education rise, then fall as educated workers become plentiful.

Evidence against. Taiwan, South Korea and Costa Rica grew with falling inequality. The cross-country inverted U largely vanishes once Latin American countries (middle-income, very unequal) are controlled for.

Conclusion. Not inevitable: the nature of growth and policy decide.
pts: States the hypothesis: inequality first rises, then falls as per capita income grows (inverted U)
Gives a mechanism: modern-sector enlargement, or rising then falling returns to education
Evidence against: counter-examples (Taiwan, Korea) or the Latin American effect
Concludes that the pattern is not inevitable; the type of growth and policy decide
6c.src: Ch 5 Poverty and inequality, slides 36, 40-43; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 279-284
6c.watch:
• Draw the axes correctly: Gini (or another inequality measure) on the vertical axis, GNI per capita on the horizontal.
  • With 5 1/3 marks, a balanced paragraph on each side is enough.

7a.html:
Human capital is the productive capacity embodied in people, built by spending on education, training and health care. Investing in it matters for these reasons:

  1. Ends in themselves. Health and education are core parts of well-being and of Sen's capabilities: a long, healthy, informed life is what development means.
  2. High returns. By the human capital approach, an investment is worth making if the present value of the extra earnings exceeds its direct and indirect costs:
\mathrm{PV} = \sum_{t} \frac{E_t - N_t}{(1+i)^t}

where E_t and N_t are earnings with and without the extra education and i is the discount rate. World average returns to primary schooling are about 18.9% (social) and 26.6% (private), above most physical investments.

  1. Productivity and growth. Educated workers absorb modern technology; healthy workers work more and better.
  2. Complementarity. They are investments in the same person: health raises the return to schooling, and education raises the return to health.
  3. Market failure. Spillovers and credit constraints mean families under-invest, and higher income alone does not fix this, so public investment is needed.
  4. Poverty, gender and population. Educating girls lowers fertility, improves child health and breaks the poverty cycle, so its social return is among the highest.

Conclusion: health and education are both goals and engines of development, so they deserve priority in public spending.
pts: Ends in themselves: core of well-being and capabilities
Human-capital approach: PV of extra earnings compared with direct and indirect costs, with the formula or a rate of return
Returns are high, for example about 19% social and 27% private for primary schooling (world)
Inputs to production: productivity, absorbing technology, growth
Complementarity: health and education raise each other's returns
Market failures and spillovers: private under-investment, so public investment is needed
Poverty, gender and fertility benefits, especially of girls' education
7a.src: Ch 8 Education and health, slides 2-5, 8, 10; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 431-438
7a.watch:
• Private returns exceed social returns, especially at higher levels, because the state pays much of the cost; primary education has the highest social return.
  • Both health and education must appear; an answer only about schooling loses about a third of the marks.

7b.html:
The claim holds when the labour market has multiple equilibria (Basu's model); otherwise a ban can make poor families worse off.

Assumptions

  1. Luxury axiom: a family sends its children to work only if adult income is too low.
  2. Substitution axiom: child and adult labour are substitutes, a child being worth \gamma < 1 adult, so labour can be counted in adult equivalents.

The model. All adults work whatever the wage (vertical supply AA'). Below the wage w_H poor families start sending children to work, so supply bends outward along an S-shaped curve; below w_L all children work (vertical TT'). If labour demand D_L is inelastic, it cuts the supply curve at two stable points: E1 (high wage, no child labour) and E2 (low wage, child labour). Child labour keeps the wage low, so families are trapped at E2 by a coordination failure: all would gain if every family withdrew its children, but none can do it alone.

Effect of a ban. An effective ban removes child labour supply and moves the market to E1. Adult wages rise enough that families no longer need child earnings, children go to school, and the ban becomes self-enforcing: children and families both gain.

Limits

  • If demand is elastic there is only one equilibrium; at a low-wage equilibrium a ban just cuts family income and may push children into worse informal work.
  • Employers lose from higher wages and resist the law; E2 can even be Pareto-optimal.
  • How common such markets are is unknown.

Conclusion: the statement is true for multiple-equilibrium markets, so the policy is a ban backed by schooling incentives (CCTs) and a ban on the worst forms first.
pts: States that the claim holds under multiple equilibria (Basu), not in general
The two assumptions: luxury axiom and substitution axiom (child equals \gamma < 1 adult)
Supply curve: vertical AA' above w_H, S-shaped between w_H and w_L, vertical TT' below w_L
Inelastic demand gives two stable equilibria, E1 (no child labour, high wage) and E2 (child labour, low wage)
A ban moves the market to E1: higher adult wage, children in school, self-enforcing; a coordination failure explained
Limits: single equilibrium with elastic demand (ban harms families), or employers' opposition and Pareto optimality
Uncertain evidence, so complementary policies (CCTs, schooling, worst forms first)
Reasoned conclusion
7b.src: Ch 8 Education and health, slide 9; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 443-447
7b.watch:
• The diagram is the clearest way to show the two equilibria; describe the curve shapes even if you do not draw them.
  • The middle crossing on the S-shaped part is unstable; only E1 and E2 are stable.
  • "Discuss" needs the limits as well; an answer that only proves the claim loses about a quarter of the marks.

8a.html:
Capital budgeting is the process of planning and evaluating long-term investment projects (new plant, machinery, expansion, infrastructure) whose costs come now and whose returns spread over several years. It decides which projects to accept or reject, how to rank them, and how to allocate a limited capital budget.

Methods

Non-discounted (traditional):

  1. Payback period: years to recover the investment, \text{investment}/\text{annual cash flow} for equal flows. Accept if within a cut-off. Simple, shows liquidity, but ignores time value and all flows after payback.
  2. Accounting rate of return (ARR): average annual accounting profit divided by average investment. Accept if above a target. Uses accounting profit, not cash flow, and ignores timing.

Discounted cash flow:

  1. NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{n} CF_t/(1+r)^t. Accept if positive. Uses all flows and time value and measures value added; the primary method.
  2. IRR: the rate at which NPV = 0. Accept if above the cost of capital. Easy to communicate, but can mis-rank projects of different scale and assumes reinvestment at the IRR.
  3. Profitability index (PI), or BCR: PV of inflows divided by the initial investment. Accept if above 1; ranks projects under capital rationing.
  4. Discounted payback: payback using discounted flows; always longer than simple payback.
pts: Defines capital budgeting: planning and evaluating long-term investments whose returns extend over several years (accept or reject, ranking, rationing)
Classifies the methods into non-discounted and discounted cash flow methods
Payback period: formula, rule, merit (liquidity) and limitation (ignores later flows and time value)
Accounting rate of return: definition, rule, limitation
NPV: formula, accept if positive, merits
IRR: rate giving NPV = 0, accept if above the cost of capital, a limitation
Profitability index or BCR: ratio above 1, use under capital rationing
Discounted payback
Concludes that NPV is the primary method

8b.html:
Given: A: USD 300,000 outlay, USD 100,000 a year for 5 years; B: USD 2,000,000 outlay, USD 600,000 a year for 5 years; discount and reinvestment rate r = 10\%.

Find: compare the five methods, with advantages and disadvantages.

Solution. The 5-year annuity factor at 10% is \sum_{t=1}^{5} 1.1^{-t} = 3.791, so the PV of inflows is USD 379,079 for A and USD 2,274,472 for B. Recomputation confirms the printed results:

MethodProject AProject BPrefers
Payback300{,}000/100{,}000 = 3.0 yr2{,}000{,}000/600{,}000 = 3.33 yrA
Discounted payback3.75 yr4.26 yrA
NPV, USD379{,}079 - 300{,}000 = 79{,}0792{,}274{,}472 - 2{,}000{,}000 = 274{,}472B
PI379{,}079/300{,}000 = 1.261.14A
IRR19.9\%15.2\%A

Both projects are acceptable (\mathrm{NPV} > 0, \mathrm{PI} > 1, \mathrm{IRR} > 10\%). Rankings conflict because of scale (B is 6.7 times larger). The increment B minus A (USD 1,700,000 for USD 500,000 a year) has NPV USD 195,393 and IRR 14.4%, so the extra investment pays.

  • Payback, discounted payback: simple liquidity screens; ignore cash after payback (plain payback also ignores time value).
  • NPV: uses all cash flows and time value, measures wealth added; needs a discount rate and does not show the return per unit invested.
  • PI: value per unit invested; can mis-rank projects of different size, as here.
  • IRR: easy percentage but assumes reinvestment at the IRR; at the given 10% the MIRR is 15.3% (A) and 12.9% (B).

Answer: choose B if the projects are mutually exclusive and funds are available (highest NPV); under capital rationing choose A (higher PI).
pts: Notes that both projects pass every test at 10% (NPV > 0, PI > 1, IRR > 10%)
Payback 3.0 against 3.33 years and discounted payback 3.75 against 4.26 years, both favouring A
NPV USD 79,079 for A and USD 274,472 for B: both acceptable, B higher
PI 1.26 against 1.14 and IRR 19.9% against 15.2%: both acceptable, A higher
Explains the conflict by scale (B about 6.7 times larger) and resolves it: incremental B minus A has NPV USD 195,393 and IRR 14.4%, above 10% (or the profiles cross at 14.4%)
Decision: B when mutually exclusive with funds available, A under capital rationing
Payback methods: simple liquidity screens but ignore cash flows after payback
NPV: all cash flows and time value, wealth in money terms; needs a discount rate and does not show return per unit invested
PI: value per unit invested, useful under capital rationing; can mis-rank projects of different size
IRR: intuitive percentage but assumes reinvestment at the IRR (MIRR at 10%: 15.3% and 12.9%) and mis-ranks by scale

8b.watch:
• The table already prints the results, so the marks are for the comparison and the reasons; do not just copy the numbers.
  • The note's 10% reinvestment rate points at the IRR assumption. IRR implies the USD 100,000 inflows are reinvested at 19.9%, which is unrealistic when capital costs 10%; MIRR fixes this.
  • The Total row (USD 200,000 and USD 1,000,000) is undiscounted net cash and is not a valid criterion.
  • 3.33 years is 3 years 4 months. Discounted payback is always longer than plain payback.
  • For mutually exclusive projects the handout's rule applies: NPV is the primary criterion, the others are supporting indicators.
